questions.question_text_en:
In a kinetic experiment, a student placed crystals of iodine in a closed reaction vessel, introduced a given quantity of 
hydrogen gas, and collected data to calculate the rate of formation of hydrogen iodide. What would be the effect obtained on 
the rate of the reaction, if the student takes more amount of iodine from that used in the first experiment?
questions.source_name: ESSLCE Chemistry 2015 E.C. National Exam Archive

choices.label: A
choices.text_en: It speeds up the rate of the reaction.

choices.label: B
choices.text_en: It lowers the rate of the reaction.

choices.label: C
choices.text_en: The formation of hydrogen iodide will be decreased.

choices.label: D
choices.text_en: The rate of the reaction will be constant.

explanation.solution_text_en:
It speeds up the rate of the reaction. Reaction rate depends on effective collisions and the slowest elementary step 
controls a multistep mechanism.

questions.question_text_en:

equilibrium position to the right?
questions.source_name: ESSLCE Chemistry 2015 E.C. National Exam Archive

replace the removed product; changing amounts of pure solids does not change the equilibrium expression.

questions.question_text_en: Which of the following is CORRECTLY stated about the spontaneity of a reaction?
questions.source_name: ESSLCE Chemistry 2015 E.C. National Exam Archive

choices.label: A
choices.text_en: For an endothermic reaction with negative reaction entropy, the reaction is spontaneous at all temperature.

choices.label: B
choices.text_en: For an exothermic reaction with positive reaction entropy, the reaction is non-spontaneous at all temperature.

choices.label: C
choices.text_en: For an endothermic reaction with positive reaction entropy, the reaction is non-spontaneous at low temperature.

choices.label: D
choices.text_en: For an exothermic reaction with negative reaction entropy, the reaction is spontaneous at high temperature.

explanation.solution_text_en:
For ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is positive at low temperature but can become negative at sufficiently high 
temperature. Therefore C is correct.
explanation.key_concept: Curriculum link: Grade 10 Chemistry — Unit 4: Energy Changes and Electrochemistry

questions.question_text_en:
Given the following: bond energies (kJ/mol) H-H 436 N-N 193 N=N 409 N≡N 942 and the enthalpy for the reaction 1 / 2 N₂ 
(g) + 3 / 2 H₂ (g) →NH₃ (g); ΔH=-45 kJ/mol What is the bond energy for NH₃?
questions.source_name: ESSLCE Chemistry 2015 E.C. National Exam Archive

explanation.solution_text_en:
Bonds broken require ½(942)+3/2(436)=1125 kJ mol⁻¹. Since ΔH = broken − formed = −45, total N–H bond energy 
formed is 1170 kJ mol⁻¹; option B.
explanation.key_concept: Curriculum link: Grade 10 Chemistry — Unit 4: Energy Changes and Electrochemistry

questions.question_text_en:
The rate law for this reaction CO (g) + NO₂ (g) → CO₂ (g) + NO (g) is rate = k [NO₂ ] p [CO] q. Which one of the following 
could be a plausible mechanism for the reaction?
questions.review_note: The stem leaves the exponents p and q unspecified. Option A is the intended mechanism for the well-known low-temperature rate law rate ∝ [NO₂]², but the item is under-specified as printed.
questions.source_name: ESSLCE Chemistry 2015 E.C. National Exam Archive

choices.label: A
choices.text_en: NO₂ (g) + NO₂ (g) -> NO 3 (g) + NO(g) [slow] NO 3 (g) + CO(g) -> NO₂ (g) + CO₂ (g) [fast]

choices.label: B
choices.text_en: NO 3 (g) + NO(g) -> NO₂ (g) + NO₂ (g) [slow] NO₂ (g) + CO₂ (g) -> NO 3 (g) + CO(g) [fast]

choices.label: C
choices.text_en: NO₂ (g) + NO(g) -> NO 3 (g) + NO₂ (g) [slow] NO 3 (g) + CO(g) -> NO₂ (g) + CO₂ (g) [fast]

choices.label: D
choices.text_en: NO₂ (g) + NO₂ (g) -> NO 3 (g) + NO(g) [fast] NO 3 (g) + CO(g) -> NO₂ (g) + CO₂ (g) [slow]

explanation.solution_text_en:
The intended known rate law for this reaction at low temperature is second order in NO₂ and independent of CO. A 
slow 2NO₂ step followed by a fast reaction of the intermediate with CO gives that behavior and the correct net reaction, so A is the 
intended mechanism.
explanation.key_concept: Curriculum link: Grade 11 Chemistry — Unit 4: Chemical Kinetics

questions.question_text_en:
Which one of the following is the main reason for the large difference in dipole-moment between the triatomic molecules 
water (H₂O) and carbon dioxide (CO₂)?
questions.review_note: The choices are imperfectly worded. The decisive chemistry is molecular geometry: H₂O is bent and has a net dipole, while linear CO₂ has canceling bond dipoles.
questions.source_name: ESSLCE Chemistry 2015 E.C. National Exam Archive

choices.label: A
choices.text_en: The presence of lone pairs of electrons in water (H₂O) partially reinforces bond polarities.

choices.label: B
choices.text_en: The higher electronegativity difference among atoms in water (H₂O) than in carbon dioxide (CO₂).

choices.label: C
choices.text_en: The presence of multiple bonds in carbon dioxide (CO₂) while single bonds in water.

choices.label: D
choices.text_en: The bonds in carbon dioxide (CO₂) are directed 180° and bond polarity reinforces each other.

explanation.solution_text_en:
CO₂ is linear, so its two C=O bond dipoles cancel. H₂O is bent because of two lone pairs on oxygen, so its O–H 
dipoles do not cancel. Option A is the closest statement among the choices.
explanation.key_concept: Curriculum link: Grade 11 Chemistry — Unit 2: Chemical Bonding

questions.question_text_en:
180 g of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) is allowed to react with 156 gram of hydrochloric acid (HCl), according to the following 
reaction. Which of the following substances is the limiting reagent? (Atomic masses; Ca=40, Cl=35.5, O=16, C=12, H=1) 
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O
questions.source_name: ESSLCE Chemistry 2015 E.C. National Exam Archive

explanation.solution_text_en:
n(CaCO₃)=180/100=1.80 mol. n(HCl)=156/36.5≈4.27 mol; 1.80 mol CaCO₃ needs 3.60 mol HCl, so CaCO₃ is 
consumed first and is the limiting reagent (B).
explanation.key_concept: Curriculum link: Grade 10 Chemistry — Unit 5: Metals and Nonmetals
